Babies get some of this already. Practical love matters a lot.
t65u_lm4p2a2: But a big spiritual experience can show you a kind of peace, or a love, you didn't know existed, and then "I want you to be happy" suddenly means something much bigger. That's partly why loving-kindness meditation can sound almost comically simple to someone who's never been near what it's pointing at, and so powerful to someone who has. t65u_lm4p3a: If you're curious about any of that, follow the curiosity instead of pretending to believe something. Read people from different traditions. Or mostly more sure they've got the right explanation?

The whole horizon of life feels too small, and a meal or a boundary or one kind sentence can help without touching the question underneath: "Why should I want this life at all?" Curiosity can be enough here, something like "People say they've felt a love I never have. I don't know if I buy their explanation, but what if it's possible for me?" What you've felt so far isn't the limit of what's possible.

## Borrow Hindsight

A question to borrow from your future self: "How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?" It can change how the whole thing looks. It can also just make you feel a bit more like that person, or less alone (sometimes all at once). Keep in mind it's only their best guess. No perfect Higher Self is handing down answers.

That future you also knows why you can't pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe they'd be kind about it, or maybe they'd just make you some food. If you can't picture them at all, make the food yourself (a "no" or a pause counts as food here), and skip pretending to feel some way you don't.

# Simple Practices

## Borrow Hindsight

A question to borrow from your future self: "How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?" It can change how the whole thing looks. It can also just make you feel a bit more like that person, or less alone (sometimes all at once). Keep in mind it's only their best guess. No perfect Higher Self is handing down answers.

That future you also knows why you can't pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe they'd be kind about it, or maybe they'd just make you some food. If you can't picture them at all, make the food yourself (a "no" or a pause counts as food here), and skip pretending to feel some way you don't.

If someone else is part of this, you can borrow a wiser future version of them, too, as long as you don't assume they'll end up on your side, or sorry. What the current one keeps doing is still what you go by, however good the picture looks (the future one has never called you back).

## Remember When You Already Did It

Somewhere in your history there's probably a time you handled something hard and came out of it respecting yourself a little. Go find it. What did you do, and what was helping you then? If one piece of that is still within reach, use it. The example can be small (it doesn't have to top this one). It's also no proof you should manage the same way today, when you might be more worn out or missing whatever helped you then. (No example? Try another way in.)

## A Heart-to-Child Loop

With a little warmth to work with, rest one hand at the center of your chest (the heart chakra) and feel for love, and the other on the solar plexus, just below, and feel for your little one. The solar plexus is the most vulnerable part of the torso, as anyone who's been hit there can tell you. So it makes sense to look for your little one there.

Picture the love traveling from your heart down to your little one. If some comes back up, let it, and send it on down again, so it goes around like a loop. That part's a gift from them, and they don't owe it to you, so if nothing comes back, just keep sending yours. No warmth today? Then rest your hands there and notice what you find, no faking required.

## “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”

Finish a hard memory with "And so that's the way it happened!" the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. ("Once upon a time…" helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.

A story ending doesn't turn the memory into fiction, and it doesn't prove it either. Nobody gets let off, and nobody's repair gets canceled. The case just stops being argued. Listen to how the narrator sounds, though, and stop if they start sneering ("...and so that's the way it happened, dummy"), or if the shame grows, or you start feeling unreal. More distance won't fix those. And if the phrase helps, keep it short and ask what the person in that story needs from you now.

## Just Like Me

This one works best on a steadier day, when thinking about other people won't pull you out of your own shoes. Name the feeling plainly. Lonely, say. Then think of how many people are feeling that exact thing right now, and wanting it to stop, just like you. Some of them make it worse trying to get away from it. Just like you, sometimes. 😅 Wish all of you, you first, enough support to stay with it, so the pain stops with you.

You don't need special breathing for it. You also don't need to forgive anyone, or picture the childhood of whoever hurt you. The wish doesn't ask you to contact them, either. Whether you ever do is a separate decision, and never one to make while you're flooded. What it does is take away the idea that a feeling this common proves you're the defective one.

## One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night

Mornings get a tiny goal: "Today I'll notice one hook before I act on it." Whichever hook it is. Then at night you take a quick look back, like you're watching the highlights with a friend. Where did you catch the hook? Where did it get you anyway? What's one small repair or protective thing for tomorrow?

## One Intention in the Morning, One Review at Night

You can bookend the day. In the morning, set one small intention, like "Today I'll notice one hook before I act on it." Any hook will do. At night, look back gently. Where did you notice one? Where did it run its whole routine before you caught on? And what's a small repair, or something protective, you could do next?

# When Love Still Feels Missing

If you weren't loved very well as a child, "love your inner child" can sound like nonsense. You might really want the best for your little one, hug them in your imagination, even miss them, and still not feel any of the warm stuff people mean when they say love. You're not broken for that. It just means starting somewhere smaller.
t65u_seclm1p1b:
# When Love Still Feels Missing

"Love your inner child" can sound like total nonsense if nobody loved you all that well when you were one. You can want good things for your little one, hug them in your head, miss them, and still feel none of that warm glow people talk about. That's a real place to start from, and it has its own way in.

## Notice the Part That Came Here

Some people hear all this about love and say, "No. I hate myself." If that's what you find in there, I don't want to argue you out of it. It deserves an honest hearing. But I don't want to skip over something else, either. If you chose to open this article, or go to therapy, or ask someone for help, or try again after you'd decided you were hopeless, something in you wanted things to be different.

## Notice the Part That Came Here

And some people go further: "No. I hate myself." If that's where you are, I'm not going to argue with it, because it deserves an honest hearing. I'd just point at one thing. You chose to read this. Maybe you also chose therapy, or asked for help, or tried again after deciding you were hopeless. Something in you wanted things to be different.
t65u_seclm3p1a2:
## Somatic Heart Opening

Rumi says you have to keep breaking your heart until it stays open. Some people find that deep grieving turns into warmth, or connection, or a feeling in the body of being held by the whole universe. The feeling is real, though it doesn't prove what the body is doing to make it. It can go the other way, too: being cared for can bring up sadness about the care you didn't get, and that doesn't mean the love failed. Stay with it while you can still be present and choose, and slow down when it starts to swamp you.
t65u_seclm3p1b:
## Somatic Heart Opening

Rumi says to keep breaking your heart until it stays open, which sounds intense, and it can be. For some people, deep grieving turns into warmth or connection, or a sense in the body of being held by the whole universe. That's real as an experience, though it doesn't tell you what's going on physically. And being cared for can bring grief up, too, for the care you never got, which doesn't mean the love failed. Go only as deep as you can while staying present and able to choose. If it starts swamping you, slow down.

## How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?

Part of love is wanting someone to be well, and how far that wish can reach depends partly on what kind of happiness you know is possible. If the happiness you know is food, safety, affection, friends, work that means something and some help when you need it, then wanting those things for somebody is love. Babies get some of this already. Practical love matters a lot.
